column4: Here's something most people never quite picture. When you buy a stock, you aren't buying a lottery ticket. You're buying a real slice of a real business. On screen, watch one company drawn as a whole pie, and one small piece lifted out and handed to an investor. That piece is yours. In the next few minutes we'll pin down exactly what a share is, and how the market that trades it actually works.

Let's define it cleanly. A stock is a security that represents proportionate ownership in a company. Buy one share and you become a shareholder, with a real claim on that company's assets and its earnings. Look at the slice on screen. Own more slices, and you own more of the pie. Some companies hand a portion of their profits back to shareholders as dividends, cash paid out on a regular schedule. And here's the part that surprises people. There's no hundred-share minimum. A single share makes you an owner.

So where do these slices change hands? The stock market isn't one building with a bell. It's a network. Follow the diagram. Buyers and sellers all over the world connect through central exchanges and the brokers that route their orders. A private company joins that network through an i.p.o., an initial public offering, the first time it sells shares to the public to raise money. After that first sale, the shares trade freely between investors on the exchange, day after day.

Now, what actually moves the price? Supply and demand, the simple tug of war between buyers and sellers. Drag the slider yourself. Push it toward more buyers and watch the price token climb, because when demand outweighs supply, the price rises. Push it toward more sellers and it slides down. Land it in the middle and the price holds steady. This is an illustrative model, not a forecast, but that push and pull is the real engine behind every tick.

You'll often hear that the market went up or down. But the market is enormous, so we track it with indexes. An index is a snapshot of one part of the market. See the three pills on screen. The Dow Jones Industrial Average follows thirty large u.s. companies. The s and p five hundred tracks the five hundred largest. And the Nasdaq Composite leans heavily toward technology names. Different baskets, each telling you how its slice of the market is doing.

Some of these sound true because you've heard them repeated so often, but repetition doesn't make them right. Think back through what we just covered before you place each one.
Five quick questions to lock it all in. Take your time, and answer each one to earn your points for the lesson.

Let's carry four things forward. A stock is real ownership, a slice of a business with a claim on its assets and earnings. Companies go public through an i.p.o., and after that their shares trade on exchanges. Price moves on supply and demand. And indexes are snapshots that tell you how a part of the market is doing. You now know what a stock is and how it trades. Next, we zoom into the price chart itself and learn to read candlestick anatomy and timeframes, the language every chart speaks.
